title: Single-Contact Problem in Atomically Flat Interfaces: a Simulation Approach
authors: Rui Dong, Ahmed Uluca, Graham Cross, Stefano Sanvito
abstract: Understanding friction at single-asperity contacts is essential for bridging the gap between nanoscale structural superlubricity and realistic tribological systems dominated by Hertzian contact geometry. In this work, we combine atomistic simulations and a modified continuum model to investigate the onset of sliding at crystalline SiO$_2$/SiO$_2$ interfaces. Interfacial sliding potential energy surfaces (ISPES) are computed to determine the load-dependent shear strength and minimal-scale sliding (MSS) friction. Both quantities exhibit linear dependence on normal pressure below 3 GPa, and have non-zero values at zero pressure. Incorporating these parameters, we extend the classical Mindlin model by including adhesion and nanoscale load effects, allowing us to describe the stick to slip transition under realistic Hertzian stress distributions. The model shows that nonuniform pressure distributions substantially lower the effective static friction, and oscillatory-shear experiments on graphene-passivated contacts reproduce both the predicted stiffness-collapse signature and, in the passivated limit, the adhesion-limited shear strength obtained from simulation, supporting the model's relevance to real micro-asperity tribology.
summary: This paper investigates friction at nanoscale contacts using crystalline SiO2/SiO2 interfaces. It develops a modified continuum model that integrates atomistic simulation results for shear strength and adhesion effects. The resulting framework successfully predicts experimental observations, particularly the stiffness collapse during sliding, demonstrating its relevance to realistic micro-tribology.
main_problem: The work aims to bridge the theoretical understanding of superlubricity at atomically flat interfaces with the reality of tribological systems governed by Hertzian contact geometry.
main_result: A modified Mindlin model, incorporating load-dependent shear strength and adhesion, successfully reproduces key experimental signatures like stiffness collapse in oscillatory shear tests on passivated contacts.
method: The study combines atomistic simulations (calculating Interfacial Sliding Potential Energy Surfaces) with the extension of classical continuum mechanics models (Mindlin's model).
model_or_system: The system studied is the friction and sliding behavior at crystalline SiO2/SiO2 interfaces. The theoretical framework uses a modified Mindlin model to account for non-uniform Hertzian stress distributions, adhesion, and load dependence.
key_observables: Load-dependent shear strength ($	au$), Minimal-Scale Sliding (MSS) friction ($\sigma$), effective lateral stiffness ($k$), and total lateral force ($Q$).
important_parameters: Normal pressure ($P$) up to 3 GPa, the adhesion-limited intercept ($	au_0$), and the critical radius defining stick/slip zones.
main_assumptions: The simulation assumes an atomically flat profile is maintained; the model extends classical frameworks by incorporating finite adhesion and load dependence, which are crucial for matching experimental results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the constant-pressure ISPES showing minimum energy pathways, radial distributions of shear stress vs. applied stress (Figure 4), and oscillatory shear response comparing bare vs. graphene-passivated contacts showing stiffness collapse (Figure 6).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for a multiscale approach by simulating ISPES to find load-dependent friction parameters ($	au, \sigma$). It then extends the Mindlin model using these parameters to predict behavior under Hertzian loading. Finally, it validates this modified model against oscillatory shear experiments.
why_interesting: While focused on solid mechanics and tribology, the development of a multiscale constitutive model that accurately captures transition regimes (stick-slip) by incorporating non-linear material properties (adhesion, load dependence) is relevant to understanding complex boundary conditions in quantum systems or interfaces where classical assumptions break down.

(a) Atomic structure of the SiO2-SiO2 flat-on-flat interfaces, and (b) top view of the “dense” surface of α-quarts SiO2. Highlighted in (b) is the six-ring reconstructed surface. Color code: silicon = blue, oxygen = red.

Figure 2: Minimum energy pathway on the constant-pressure ISPES and the energy and force profiles at 0.5 GPa normal load. (a) The constant-pressure ISPES of SiO2-SiO2 flat- on-flat interface. The white line shows the minimum energy pathway and the red dotted lines denotes the rectangular 1×2 supercell. Panel (b) shows the energy profile along the pathway. Zero energy is associated to the global energy minimum obtained at zero normal load. Red arrows mark the energy loss to overcome each barrier. Figure 3: The shear strength, τ, and the coefficient of friction in minimal-scale sliding, σ, are plotted against the normal load, p, together with their linear fit. Here both τ and σ are extracted from the constant-pressure ISPES. Both quantities have a linear dependence on the external load in the low pressure limit.

Figure 4: Demonstration of the modified Mindlin model for atomically flat contacts. (a) For SiO2-SiO2 contact at 1GPa, the radial distribution of shear strength and shear stress of fully stick contact with lateral displacement of 0.2 nm. The crossover shows the boundary of stick zone. (b) Demonstration of the stick zone (red) and sliding zone (blue). (c) Demonstration of atomic scale asperities (atomic level corrugation) at the boundary.

Figure 5: SiO2-SiO2 interface sliding characteristics obtained from the modified Mindlin model at various normal pressures. (a) Total lateral force versus sliding distance of single strike sliding. When the lateral displacement increases, the lateral stress in the stick zone increases causing the stick zone to shrink. Total lateral force reaches a maximum then dropping to a constant sliding force. (b) Effective lateral stiffness in oscillation at various normal loads.
